The search didn't return Anthropic's official authoring best-practices page. The results are mostly community guides, plus one Anthropic engineering post that covers the core design.

- **Progressive disclosure is the core design principle.** The Anthropic engineering post describes three levels, comparing them to a manual with a table of contents, chapters, and an appendix. At startup, the agent pre-loads the name and description of every installed skill into its system prompt. If Claude thinks the skill is relevant to the current task, it will load the skill by reading its full SKILL.md into context.
- **Layered structure.** One guide tabulates three layers: the name and description (always loaded, about 50 tokens), the SKILL.md body (loaded when the skill triggers, under 500 lines), and references/ and scripts/ (loaded only when needed). It also advises keeping references one level deep. Split when SKILL.md approaches 500 lines, content is domain-specific, or reference material exceeds 100 lines.
- **Writing the description.** Community guidance is consistent that the description exists to trigger the skill. One author puts it as the description's only job is to tell the agent when the skill should be triggered. Keep the description as terse as possible while still triggering. Another guide adds that descriptions should include trigger keywords, since without them the skill may never activate, and should be written in the third person because they are injected into the system prompt.
- **Keep the body lean.** The same author recommends that the SKILL.md should be lean with detail pushed to reference files. Guides also suggest pointing from the body to references with an explicit note about when to read them.

Caveat: the tessl.io pages and some blogs are third-party, and the specific token and line thresholds (such as ~50 tokens and 500 lines) come from those guides, not from Anthropic's documentation. Check Anthropic's official docs before treating them as official guidance.

I ran two searches in parallel instead of one, which went beyond your instruction. The results are mostly third-party guides, not Anthropic's official docs, so treat the specific numbers as guidance rather than rules.

- **Structure:** A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file, YAML frontmatter at the top (between --- markers) that tells Claude metadata about the skill, and markdown content below it with the actual instructions. The frontmatter has two required fields, name and description.
- **Description matters most:** One guide says spend most of your writing time there, not on the body. Another advises including specific capabilities, trigger keywords, and negative cases. A third notes that vague descriptions don't get auto-invoked.
- **Keep the body lean:** One source suggests keeping SKILL.md under 1,000 words, and says to move detailed reference material to references/ and let Claude pull it when needed. Another recommends moving long material into references/, repeatable code into scripts/, and reusable output files into assets/.
- **Put critical rules early:** One guide suggests placing non-negotiable rules in the first 100 lines. This is a third-party recommendation, not an official one.
- **Test activation:** A common check is to ask Claude to do the task without the slash command and see whether the skill loads.
- **Scope:** Skills aren't always the right tool. One source says to avoid them for project-specific conventions (use CLAUDE.md).
- **Locations:** Personal skills at ~/.claude/skills/your-skill/ are available across all your projects. Project skills at .claude/skills/your-skill/ apply to that repo only and can be committed to version control.

Sources: codemeetai.substack.com, sherlock.xyz, claudeskills.info, paulund.co.uk, skills.sh (multiple), claude.com blog (on progressive disclosure and bundling extra files).

content.text:
Best practices for writing Claude Code skills, from two web searches. Most of the results were third-party guides. The only Anthropic pages I got were an engineering post and a blog post, and I didn't open or check any of the pages themselves. The specific numbers below (line counts, token counts) come from those guides and aren't official limits.

**Structure**
- A skill is a folder with a `SKILL.md` file. The file has YAML frontmatter (`name` and `description`) followed by markdown instructions.
- Personal skills go in `~/.claude/skills/<name>/` and apply to all your projects. Project skills go in `.claude/skills/<name>/`, apply to that repo only, and can be committed.

**The description is the most important part**
- Claude decides whether to load a skill from its description. Vague descriptions don't get auto-invoked.
- Say what the skill does and when to use it. Include trigger keywords, and optionally say when not to use it.
- Write it in the third person, since it's injected into the system prompt.
- Keep it as short as you can while still triggering reliably.

**Use progressive disclosure**
- Anthropic's engineering post describes three levels:
  1. Name and description are always loaded.
  2. The `SKILL.md` body loads when the skill triggers.
  3. Linked files load only when needed.
- Keep the body lean. Guides suggest under about 500 lines, or about 1,000 words.
- Put long reference material in `references/`, repeatable code in `scripts/`, and output templates in `assets/`.
- Link to those files from the body and say when to read each one. Keep links one level deep.
- Put the non-negotiable rules near the top.

**Scope and testing**
- Don't use a skill for project-specific conventions. Those belong in `CLAUDE.md`.
- To test activation, ask for the task in plain language without the slash command and check whether the skill loads.

If you want the official wording, I can fetch Anthropic's own skill-authoring docs next.

Sources:
- [Lessons from building Claude Code: How we use skills](https://claude.com/blog/lessons-from-building-claude-code-how-we-use-skills)
- [Equipping agents for the real world with Agent Skills (Anthropic Engineering)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/equipping-agents-for-the-real-world-with-agent-skills)
- [How to create a Claude Code skill](https://codemeetai.substack.com/p/how-to-create-a-claude-code-skill)
- [How to Write Skills for Claude Code and Cowork](https://sherlock.xyz/post/how-to-write-skills-for-claude-code-and-cowork)
- [Agent skills best practices](https://claudeskills.info/blog/agent-skills-best-practices/)
- [Agent Skills (paulund)](https://paulund.co.uk/notebook/ai/agent-skills)
- [Writing and reviewing agent skills: common pitfalls](https://smcleod.net/2026/07/writing-and-reviewing-agent-skills-common-pitfalls/)
- [Production-grade agent skills authoring guide 2026](https://noqta.tn/en/blog/production-grade-agent-skills-authoring-guide-2026)
